$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$

The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-8.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D=P^T \! A P.$
current_example.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D=P^TAP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=5\quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-8$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224380/assets/429eefda5abcd90f45f89c304e1c829464bf349ada6dce323919482a5486ffa0.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224380/assets/2c2a940befb263f02df50987f7ba0e89ee2b29b727ad5168972057c0542adb68.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]+8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224380/assets/fbe5fc3943c7b0d94407fd48f32548308b56f98c66a4c75808b912769219dea5.svg) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{13},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224380/assets/57f5da15c0c4f285e7961a894dd2fc6e1511c73a2e2249483847cd7416d01cb4.svg)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
